real_life_application.question: A force (1, 1) pulls on an object; which displacement direction produces zero work?
real_life_application.explanation: Force F does no work on v when F·v = 0; (1, 1)·(1, −1) = 0 gives the perpendicular direction.

real_life_application.question: A river flows along (1, 1); which heading lets a boat drift with no upstream work?
real_life_application.explanation: A heading perpendicular to current leaves the rowing component orthogonal to flow; only downstream drift remains.

real_life_application.question: A level curve has gradient ∇f = (1, 1); the tangent direction at every point is which?
real_life_application.explanation: The gradient is normal to level sets, so the tangent must be perpendicular to (1, 1), namely along (1, −1).

real_life_application.question: Wind along (1, 1) is trimmed on a glider; which motion remains untrimmed?
real_life_application.explanation: Wind parallel to (1, 1) is trimmed out; only motions perpendicular to (1, 1), like (1, −1), survive trimming.

real_life_application.question: A sail aligned along which direction produces no useful thrust in wind (1, 1)?
real_life_application.explanation: Wind contributes no component along (1, −1); a sail aligned perpendicular to (1, 1) generates no thrust.

real_life_application.question: A budget line p₁x + p₂y = m with p₁ = p₂ = 1 has normal direction which vector?
real_life_application.explanation: The coefficients of (x, y) in p·v = constant form a normal; here (1, 1) is the budget normal.

real_life_application.question: Solving x + y = 0 gives the allowed direction set which line?
real_life_application.explanation: Equation x + y = 0 rearranges to y = −x, a diagonal line through origin.

real_life_application.question: Constraint x + y = 0 with x = t gives general solution in which form?
real_life_application.explanation: Substituting x = t forces y = −t, giving the parametric solution (t, −t).

real_life_application.question: An economist solves 1·x + 1·y = 0; the solution set is best described as which?
real_life_application.explanation: A single linear equation in two unknowns defines a 1D line; here it passes through origin.

real_life_application.question: Equation p − ρc = 0 rewritten as [1, −1]·[p, ρc] = 0 specifies which object?
real_life_application.explanation: [1, −1]·v = 0 specifies the set of (p, ρc) on a constraint line inside the 2D state space.

real_life_application.question: A workshop varies constraint 2x + 3y = 0; the permitted line of (x, y) does what?
real_life_application.explanation: Different (a, b) yield different normals; every null-space line passes through origin and rotates.

real_life_application.question: A grocer varies price vectors (p₁, p₂); null spaces p·v = 0 sweep which family?
real_life_application.explanation: Varying (a, b) over non-zero vectors makes the null-line rotate through every direction through origin.

real_life_application.question: For varying constraint a·x + b·y = 0, the perpendicular direction to (a, b) is spanned by which?
real_life_application.explanation: Rotating (a, b) by 90° gives (−b, a), and (a, b)·(−b, a) = −ab + ba = 0 confirms perpendicularity.

real_life_application.question: The locus of all null-space lines of a·x + b·y = 0 is best described as which object?
real_life_application.explanation: Lines through origin are parameterised by direction alone, giving the real projective line ℝP¹ (a circle topologically).

real_life_application.question: In a linear optimiser, the map (a, b) ↦ (−b, a) is which classical matrix operation?
real_life_application.explanation: The map (a, b) → (−b, a) is exactly a 90° rotation, producing perpendicular solution directions.

topics.title: Vectors (x, y, z) with [1, 2, 3]·[x, y, z]ᵀ = 0

real_life_application.question: A structural plane x + 2y + 3z = 0 has which normal vector in ℝ³?
real_life_application.explanation: The coefficients (a, b, c) in ax + by + cz = 0 form the normal; here n = (1, 2, 3).

real_life_application.question: A lattice point (3, 0, −1) satisfies x + 2y + 3z = 0 because the sum equals which?
real_life_application.explanation: Plugging in: 3 + 2·0 + 3·(−1) = 3 + 0 − 3 = 0, so the point sits on the constraint plane.

real_life_application.question: A basis for vectors on plane x + 2y + 3z = 0 is naturally given by which pair?
real_life_application.explanation: Both vectors satisfy the plane equation and are linearly independent, giving a 2D basis for the null space.

real_life_application.question: A force-balance reduces to x + 2y + 3z = 0; the allowed (x, y, z) set is which?
real_life_application.explanation: One linear equation in three unknowns defines a 2D plane, and the zero constant keeps origin on it.

real_life_application.question: A linear economic model restricts trade by x + 2y + 3z = 0; the perpendicular normal is which?
real_life_application.explanation: The normal (1, 2, 3) encodes the constraint and is perpendicular to every point of the plane.

real_life_application.question: An object moves with velocity (1, 2, 1) m/s; at t = 3 its position is which point?
real_life_application.explanation: Position = t·(1, 2, 1) at t = 3 gives (3, 6, 3) along the parametric line T.

real_life_application.question: A force along (1, 2, 1) acts through origin; the line of action parameterises by which scalar?
real_life_application.explanation: Lines through origin are spanned by the direction vector (1, 2, 1) and traced by α·(1, 2, 1).

real_life_application.question: A satellite follows direction (1, 2, 1) through origin; which point is on its trajectory?
real_life_application.explanation: (2, 4, 2) = 2·(1, 2, 1) is a scalar multiple, so it lies on T; the others are not collinear with (1, 2, 1).

real_life_application.question: A wire carries current along (1, 2, 1) through origin; positions T form which subspace?
real_life_application.explanation: T = span{(1, 2, 1)} is 1D because a single non-zero vector spans exactly one line through origin.

real_life_application.question: Along parametric line (t, 2t, t), which pair of coordinate ratios stays constant?
real_life_application.explanation: From (x, y, z) = (t, 2t, t) we get y = 2x and z = x, so y:x = 2 and z:x = 1 along T.

real_life_application.question: A drone flies along (2, 7, 3) from origin; at β = 2 its position is which point?
real_life_application.explanation: Position = 2·(2, 7, 3) = (4, 14, 6), matching the parametric form β·(2, 7, 3).

real_life_application.question: A galvanometer reads current (2, 7, 3) on a wire; which point lies on the line through origin?
real_life_application.explanation: (6, 21, 9) = 3·(2, 7, 3) is a scalar multiple, so it sits on span{(2, 7, 3)}; the others fail the test.

real_life_application.question: A photon beam travels along (2, 7, 3); positions it occupies form which subspace?
real_life_application.explanation: A single direction spans a 1D line S = span{(2, 7, 3)}; this line passes through origin.

real_life_application.question: Along the line (2β, 7β, 3β), the ratio y to z stays which value?
real_life_application.explanation: From (2β, 7β, 3β), the ratio y:z = 7β:3β = 7:3 for any non-zero β.

real_life_application.question: A basis for S in ℝ³ is best given as which set?
real_life_application.explanation: A single non-zero vector already spans a 1D line; {(2, 7, 3)} alone forms the minimal basis for S.

real_life_application.question: Two joint axes (1, 2, 1) and (2, 7, 3) span plane W; W is which object?
real_life_application.explanation: Two linearly independent vectors in ℝ³ span a 2D plane through origin, so the arm directions fill a plane.

real_life_application.question: For directions (1, 2, 1) and (2, 7, 3) spanning W, a normal vector is which?
real_life_application.explanation: Cross product (1, 2, 1) × (2, 7, 3) = (−1, −1, 3), perpendicular to both spanning vectors.

real_life_application.question: A 2-axis gantry along (1, 2, 1) and (2, 7, 3); the equation of plane W is which?
real_life_application.explanation: Dotting the normal (−1, −1, 3) with (x, y, z) gives −x − y + 3z = 0, the equation of plane through origin.

real_life_application.question: A 2D crystal plane is spanned by (1, 2, 1) and (2, 7, 3); the dimension of W is which?
real_life_application.explanation: Two independent vectors in ℝ³ span a 2D subspace, so dim(W) = 2.

real_life_application.question: Two forces (1, 2, 1) and (2, 7, 3) act through origin; their combinations form which?
real_life_application.explanation: Two independent vectors generate a 2D plane of resultants; α(1, 2, 1) + β(2, 7, 3) lies on it.

topics.title: Vectors in W perpendicular to (w₁, w₂, w₃)

real_life_application.question: An engineer needs a normal line to plane W = span{(1, 2, 1), (2, 7, 3)}; that line is spanned by which?
real_life_application.explanation: Cross product (1, 2, 1) × (2, 7, 3) = (−1, −1, 3), a 1D direction orthogonal to both vectors in W.

real_life_application.question: In a 3D sensing app, vectors orthogonal to every vector of W form a subspace of which dim?
real_life_application.explanation: W is 2D in ℝ³, so W⊥ has dimension 3 − 2 = 1, a single line through origin.

real_life_application.question: Solving x + 2y + z = 0 and 2x + 7y + 3z = 0 for the perpendicular line yields which?
real_life_application.explanation: Eliminating x from both equations back-substitutes to v = (1, 1, −3), the perpendicular basis.

real_life_application.question: Two non-collinear forces (1, 2, 1) and (2, 7, 3) span plane W; a force perpendicular to both lies along which?
real_life_application.explanation: Cross product gives (1, 1, −3) (up to scalar), a 1D line perpendicular to both forces.

real_life_application.question: A least-squares residual r is perpendicular to every column of A; this forces r into which subspace?
real_life_application.explanation: By the fundamental theorem, the residual belongs to the orthogonal complement of the row space, W⊥.

real_life_application.question: In regression, collinear predictors cause which property for design matrix A?
real_life_application.explanation: Collinear predictors make A rank-deficient, so det(A) = 0 and the matrix is non-invertible.

real_life_application.question: A 3×3 matrix A has rows in arithmetic progression; a non-zero null vector of A is which?
real_life_application.explanation: Computing A·(1, −2, 1)ᵀ = (0, 0, 0) confirms this vector lies in the null space.

real_life_application.question: A finite-difference operator matrix A has rows in arithmetic progression; rank of A is which?
real_life_application.explanation: Three arithmetic-progression rows have only two independent ones, so rank(A) = 2.

real_life_application.question: A chemistry matrix loses rank from a balance error; the hidden null vector is which?
real_life_application.explanation: (1, −2, 1) is the non-zero null vector revealing the hidden conservation law from rank loss.

real_life_application.question: A Hankel-style matrix from arithmetic progression has null space best described as which?
real_life_application.explanation: Rank 2 in ℝ³ leaves nullity 1, so the null space is a single line through origin.

topics.title: Row space, Column space, Null space of A

real_life_application.question: For A with arithmetic-progression rows, C(A) is spanned by at most how many columns?
real_life_application.explanation: Rank is 2, so at most two columns are linearly independent and span the column space C(A).

real_life_application.question: In a network with incidence matrix A, conservation laws live in which subspace?
real_life_application.explanation: Null space vectors sum to zero across cuts; they encode conserved quantities in N(A).

real_life_application.question: For A with arithmetic-progression rows, R(A) in ℝ³ is a plane whose normal is which?
real_life_application.explanation: (1, −2, 1) ∈ N(A) is orthogonal to R(A), serving as the plane's perpendicular normal in ℝ³.

real_life_application.question: In regression y = A·x, hidden unobservable patterns in the inputs live in which subspace?
real_life_application.explanation: Adding a null-space vector to x leaves y unchanged, so N(A) hides unobservable modes.

real_life_application.question: For a 3×3 rank-2 matrix, dim C(A) + dim N(Aᵀ) equals which value?
real_life_application.explanation: For any m×n matrix, dim C(A) + dim N(Aᵀ) = m; here m = 3, so the pair sums to 3.

topics.title: Every vector of R is perpendicular to every vector of N

real_life_application.question: Residual r of fitted model is perpendicular to every column of A; r must lie in which subspace?
real_life_application.explanation: Aᵀ·r = 0 is the normal equation defining N(Aᵀ), guaranteeing r ⊥ C(A).

real_life_application.question: In regression, parameter space R(Aᵀ) and residual space N(A) in ℝⁿ satisfy which relationship?
real_life_application.explanation: By the fundamental theorem, R(Aᵀ) ⊥ N(A) and together they decompose ℝⁿ into complementary pieces.

real_life_application.question: In PDE theory, the kernel of a symmetric elliptic operator is orthogonal to which subspace?
real_life_application.explanation: Self-adjoint operators have ranges perpendicular to their kernels under the standard inner product.

real_life_application.question: Eigenspaces of a Hermitian operator for distinct eigenvalues are related how?
real_life_application.explanation: Hermitian operators have orthogonal eigenspaces — a physical realisation of R(A) ⊥ N(A).

real_life_application.question: Signal processing separates 'signal' from 'noise' using which pair of orthogonal subspaces?
real_life_application.explanation: Signal lives in column space C(A); noise is the perpendicular left-null piece N(Aᵀ).

topics.title: B takes line 2y + x = 4 to where?

real_life_application.question: A projection lens B = [[1, 2], [2, 4]] maps line x + 2y = 4 to which screen point?
real_life_application.explanation: For any (x, y) on x + 2y = 4, B·(x, y) = (4, 2·4) = (4, 8); the line collapses to one point.

real_life_application.question: A camera uses B = [[1, 2], [2, 4]]; the line x + 2y = 4 lands on which pixel?
real_life_application.explanation: Rank-deficient B sends every point on the parallel-to-kernel line to a single image spot (4, 8).

real_life_application.question: A lossy encoder uses rank-1 matrix B; line x + 2y = 4 is encoded as which single codeword?
real_life_application.explanation: Parallel lines to the kernel collapse to single outputs; here x + 2y = 4 yields code (4, 8).

real_life_application.question: A 3D shadow loses depth: line x + 2y = 4 projects via B to which shadow spot?
real_life_application.explanation: Each line parallel to N(B) collapses to one shadow; x + 2y = 4 under B yields the spot (4, 8).

real_life_application.question: A bad microphone mixes inputs via B; any signal on x + 2y = 4 produces which output?
real_life_application.explanation: B·(x, y) only depends on s = x + 2y, so s = 4 yields the fixed output (4, 8).

topics.title: B takes 2y + x = k to where?

real_life_application.question: A factory robot uses B = [[1, 2], [2, 4]]; inputs satisfying x + 2y = k produce which image?
real_life_application.explanation: B·(x, y) = (x + 2y, 2(x + 2y)) = (k, 2k); every k-fibre lands at the point (k, 2k).

real_life_application.question: An engineer varies constant k in x + 2y = k; the image point traces which locus?
real_life_application.explanation: As k changes, the image point (k, 2k) slides along y = 2x, sweeping out that entire line.

real_life_application.question: A sensor reads scalar k = x + 2y and reconstructs a 2D point by which formula?
real_life_application.explanation: Reconstruction multiplies the scalar k by direction (1, 2), giving the 2D point (k, 2k).

real_life_application.question: A linear encoder with B = [[1, 2], [2, 4]] produces code c = (c₁, c₂); the encoded scalar is which?
real_life_application.explanation: The first code component c₁ equals x + 2y, the value of the 1D fibre; c₂ = 2c₁ adds no new info.

real_life_application.question: For the 1D subspace spanned by (1, 2), the matrix B acts as which kind of map?
real_life_application.explanation: B = (1, 2)ᵀ·(1, 2) projects inputs onto span{(1, 2)}, preserving that direction exactly.

real_life_application.question: A classifier uses B = [[1, 2], [2, 4]]; the achievable outputs form which subspace?
real_life_application.explanation: Column space C(B) = span{(1, 2)}, the line y = 2x; rank 1 restricts outputs to that line.

real_life_application.question: A regression uses design matrix B = [[1, 2], [2, 4]]; the prediction space is which?
real_life_application.explanation: Predictions B·x live in C(B) = span{(1, 2)}, exactly the prediction subspace y = 2x.

real_life_application.question: A feature map sends 2D inputs to 1D scalars; the back-mapped feature space equals which?
real_life_application.explanation: The image of B = (1, 2)ᵀ·(1, 2) is span{(1, 2)}; features can only live on that direction.

real_life_application.question: A covariance estimate of rank 1 lives in a 1D variance space spanned by which?
real_life_application.explanation: A rank-1 covariance has range span{(1, 2)}; only that direction carries variance information.

real_life_application.question: A sensor uses B = [[1, 2], [2, 4]]; which observation is NOT in the range?
real_life_application.explanation: Points (2, 4), (1, 2), and (0, 0) satisfy y = 2x, but (3, 5) fails 5 ≠ 6, so it is not in the range.

real_life_application.question: A compression algorithm replaces B by a rank-1 approximation; geometrically, B does which action?
real_life_application.explanation: Rank 1 in 2D drops one dimension: B 'squeezes' the plane onto the line y = 2x.

real_life_application.question: A recommendation matrix B has rank 1; users' vectors collapse onto which kind of subspace?
real_life_application.explanation: Rank 1 forces every output onto a 1D line through origin; B collapses 2D inputs to 1D outputs.

real_life_application.question: A smoothing filter uses singular B; the input component parallel to N(B) maps to which output?
real_life_application.explanation: Anything in the kernel of B is killed: B·v = 0 for v ∈ N(B), so that direction vanishes.

real_life_application.question: A feature embedding uses B of rank 1; features live in a space of which intrinsic dimension?
real_life_application.explanation: Rank equals the intrinsic dimension of the output; rank 1 embeddings live in a 1D subspace.

real_life_application.question: Gene expression data is approximately rank 1 because responses are linearly correlated; the approximation effectively does which action?
real_life_application.explanation: Low-rank structure shows that one 'major pattern' suffices — one dimension collapses out of the data.
